lesson.title: A Field Guide to the Usual Suspects: Common Sources of Bias
lesson.summary: Most bias in real surveys and studies falls into a handful of recognizable patterns, including undercoverage, nonresponse, response bias, and wording effects, each of which distorts results in its own characteristic way.
lesson.body:
Once bias is understood as a systematic distortion built into a method, it becomes useful to have names for the specific ways that distortion tends to creep in. Four sources appear again and again in AP Statistics and in real research: undercoverage, nonresponse bias, response bias, and wording bias. Learning to recognize each one by its signature makes it possible to diagnose a flawed study quickly rather than vaguely calling it unreliable.

Undercoverage happens when some part of the population has little or no chance of being selected by the sampling method at all, before anyone even responds. The landline-only phone survey from the discussion of bias is a textbook case of undercoverage, since cell-phone-only households are excluded from the sampling frame entirely, not merely less likely to answer. Undercoverage is a flaw in who could possibly be reached, and it exists even if everyone who is reached responds honestly and fully.

Nonresponse bias is different: it arises when people who are selected for the sample fail to respond, and the people who do respond differ systematically from those who do not. Suppose a school emails a satisfaction survey to all 800 students and only 120 respond; if students who are unhappy with the school are less likely to bother filling out a voluntary survey than students who are content, the 120 responses will paint a rosier picture than the true opinion of all 800 students, even though every one of the 800 technically had a chance to answer. Mail and email surveys are especially prone to this, since response rates are often quite low and rarely random with respect to opinion.

Response bias covers distortions that occur even when someone does respond, often because the presence of the interviewer, the sensitivity of the topic, or the desire to look good changes what the respondent reports. A classic example is a survey about illegal drug use conducted through a face to face interview, where respondents may underreport actual use because they are embarrassed or worried about consequences, even if they were told the survey was confidential. Closely related is wording bias, where the specific phrasing of a question nudges answers in a particular direction. Asking, do you support the government wasting money on unnecessary regulations, will produce far fewer yes responses than asking, do you support regulations that protect consumer safety, even though both questions could be probing the same underlying policy.

These four sources are not mutually exclusive; a single poorly designed study can suffer from more than one at once, and part of the analytical skill this course develops is asking, for any given study, which specific mechanism is most likely responsible for a suspected distortion, rather than reaching for the single, vague label of bad sample. Naming the mechanism precisely, undercoverage versus nonresponse versus response bias versus wording bias, is also what points toward the fix: a broader sampling frame addresses undercoverage, follow-up contact and incentives address nonresponse, anonymous data collection addresses response bias, and neutral, carefully piloted phrasing addresses wording bias.
